q-15717.solution:
First, we apply the constant factor rule and take the coefficient $\frac{@@n@@}{3}$ out of the integral. Then we compute the integral of $\frac{1}{x},$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{@@n@@}{3x}\text{d}x & =\frac{@@n@@}{3}\int \frac{1}{x}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{@@n@@}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=\frac{@@n@@}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $\frac{@@n@@}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{@@n@@}{3x}\text{d}x & =\frac{@@n@@}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\  & =\frac{@@n@@}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\frac{@@n@@}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =\frac{@@n@@}{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =\frac{@@n@@}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

q-103375.solution:
Expanding the binomial and applying the sum and constant factor rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1+\frac{@@n@@}{2x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =\int (1+\frac{@@n@@}{x}+\frac{@@square@@}{4{x}^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+@@n@@\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\frac{@@square@@}{4}\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+@@n@@ln⁡|x|+\frac{@@square@@{x}^{-2+1}}{4(-2+1)}+C \\  & =x+@@n@@ln⁡|x|-\frac{@@square@@}{4x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=@@n@@ln⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $@@n@@ln⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(1+\frac{@@n@@}{2x})}^{2}\text{d}x & =x-\frac{@@square@@}{4x}+@@n@@ln⁡|x|+@@n@@ln⁡K \\  & =x-\frac{@@square@@}{4x}+@@n@@(ln⁡|x|+ln⁡K) \\  & =x-\frac{@@square@@}{4x}+@@n@@ln⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$

q-103605.solution:
We separate the integrand into the sum of two fractions so that we can simplify each term. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{@@n@@x-1}{x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{@@n@@x}{x}-\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (@@n@@-\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =@@n@@\int \,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =@@n@@x-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, let's rewrite the constant so that we can combine it with the natural logarithm. For any constant $C,$ we can always write $C=-\operatorname{ln}⁡K$ where $K$ is some other positive constant. Doing this allows us to combine the constant with $-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|$ term, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{@@n@@x-1}{x}\,\text{d}x & =@@n@@x-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+C \\  & =@@n@@x-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\operatorname{ln}⁡K \\  & =@@n@@x-(\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|+\operatorname{ln}⁡K) \\  & =@@n@@x-\operatorname{ln}⁡(K|x|).\end{aligned}
$$
